title: Honest dealing
hookLine: no cheating, no hiding faults in goods (Muslim)
tomorrow: when exactly do you owe someone their pay?

cards: Online listings have a language of their own. Gently used. Minor wear.
Works great. Now a market stall, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ passes a heap of grain and pushes his hand into it.
His fingers come out wet. Rain fell on it, the seller says. That's true.
He didn't lie, and the rain wasn't his fault. And still the Prophet calls it cheating. Why?

teach.b: Here's what he said: why didn't you put the wet part on top, so people could see it? Whoever cheats is not of me. The word he uses is ghashsha, to cheat.
And the seller's wrong wasn't the rain. It was the arrangement: dry grain on top, the flaw underneath. He never said a false word.
He let the heap say it for him. That's the puzzle solved.
Cheating here isn't only lying. It's hiding.

A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says it from the other side: if buyer and seller tell the truth and make things clear, their deal is blessed; if they hide things and lie, the blessing of the deal is wiped out.
Notice the pair. Tell the truth, and make things clear. Two duties, not one, and you can keep the first and still fail the second.
So, the modern stall. Minor wear, when the zipper's broken. The photo taken from the good side.
The noise in the car nobody asked about. None of it is quite a lie. All of it is wet grain at the bottom.
One to tell a friend: the Prophet checked the grain with his own hand.

how: Muslim traders are taught to point out defects in goods before a sale; a hidden fault can give the buyer the right to undo the deal, and honest disclosure is treated as part of a blessed trade.

o: trading with nothing about the goods hidden
selling only to people of your own faith
never haggling over the price of anything

games.q: the stall and the lesson — tap the pairs.

s: in the hadith, the grain seller told a lie
he said rain fell on it, which was true. the cheat was hiding the wet part underneath.
a hadith says hiding a flaw wipes out a deal's blessing
if they tell the truth and make things clear, the deal is blessed; if they hide and lie, its blessing is wiped out.

games.q: you're selling your bike online. the gears slip in the rain; on a dry test ride nobody would notice. what does the wet grain say?
o: list it as is; the test ride is the buyer's chance to check.
put the slipping gears in the listing, right up top.
drop the price a little and say nothing; the discount covers it.
games.why: the grain seller didn't lie either. the Prophet asked why the wet part wasn't on top, so people could see it.

practice: Choose one thing you own that you might sell or lend someday. On paper, write its honest listing in two lines, the flaw first. Read it back once, and sit with it for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Honest dealing: buying and selling with the truth told and the flaw in plain sight. Not only no lies; nothing hidden.

orig.note: Arabic: cheating, deceit. 'whoever cheats (ghashsha) is not of me.'

carryVoice: For the road: nothing hidden, the wet grain on top where anyone can see it. That's two of ten.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 102 (the heap of wet grain: 'why didn't you put it on top so people could see it? whoever cheats is not of me')
Sahih al-Bukhari 2079 (if buyer and seller tell the truth and make things clear, the sale is blessed; if they hide and lie, its blessing is wiped out)
